about.title: About | Eolietech
about.description: Eolietech is a set of private file tools made by candygoogy, a developer from the Aeolian Islands. Why it runs in your browser, and why the code is open source.
about.lede: A set of file tools that work without uploading your files, made by one developer from the Aeolian Islands.
about.origin.p1: Eolietech is made by candygoogy (that's the handle), a developer from the Isole Eolie, the volcanic Aeolian Islands off the north coast of Sicily. The name comes from there: Eolie, plus tech.
about.origin.p2: The islands are where the project comes from, not what it sells. The site itself is black, white and grey, so your files and the tools stay in front. Two colours come from the islands: the deep teal of the Tyrrhenian Sea, used for links and buttons, and the orange of Stromboli's lava at night, kept for the logo.
about.palette.label: The palette
about.privacy.p1: Most online file tools upload your file to a server, process it there and send the result back. That asks for a lot of trust when the file is a scanned ID, a signed contract or a voice memo, and you can't see what happens to it on the other side.
about.privacy.p2: Browsers can now do this work themselves. Compressing an image, merging PDFs or even running a speech model is fast enough on an ordinary laptop or phone. So Eolietech does the work there, and your file never has to travel.
about.open.p1: A privacy promise you can't check is only a promise. The code is licensed under AGPL-3.0, so anyone can read what each tool does, run it themselves or point out a problem.
about.open.p2: The AGPL also means that anyone who runs a modified copy as a public service has to publish their changes under the same licence.
about.money.p1: The free tools cost very little to run, because your device does the work. A paid plan, Pro, will come later for features that need servers, such as large AI models and an API. There are no ads.

security.title: Security: check that your files stay private | Eolietech
security.description: How to confirm that Eolietech never uploads your files: the Content-Security-Policy header, the Network panel test, the offline test and the open source code.
security.lede: Eolietech says your files never leave your device. This page shows how to confirm that with nothing but your browser.
security.how.p1: When you choose a file, the tool reads it inside the page and processes it with code running on your device, often compiled to WebAssembly. The result is created in your browser and saved straight to your downloads. The file is never sent to a server.
security.csp.p1: Every page on eolietech.com is sent with a Content-Security-Policy header: a set of rules your browser enforces on the page, whatever the page's own code tries to do. For your files, the rule that matters is this one:
security.csp.p2: It means scripts on the page can only open network connections (fetch, XHR, WebSockets, beacons) to eolietech.com itself. If any code tried to send data to another server, the browser would block the request and log an error in the console.
security.csp.caveat: To be precise: 'self' still allows connections to eolietech.com. The only server endpoint on the site is the Pro waitlist sign-up, which accepts an email address. The network test below shows that the tools don't call it, or anything else, with your files.
security.csp.view: To see the header, open your browser's developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac), select the Network tab, reload the page, select the first request and find content-security-policy under Response Headers. From a terminal:
security.csp.full: The full policy, as served today:
security.csp.rule.script: script-src: code can only come from eolietech.com, plus Cloudflare Turnstile for the waitlist spam check. 'wasm-unsafe-eval' lets the tools run WebAssembly.
security.csp.rule.worker: worker-src: the background workers that do the heavy lifting must come from eolietech.com.
security.csp.rule.media: img-src and media-src: images and audio can only come from the site itself, or from data: and blob: URLs, which hold your own files in memory.
security.csp.rule.frame: frame-src: the Turnstile check is the only thing that can be embedded.
security.csp.rule.form: form-action: forms can only submit to eolietech.com.
security.network.s1: Open a tool page, then open developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac).
security.network.s2: Select the Network tab and clear the list.
security.network.s4: Look at the requests. The first time you use a tool you may see its code, WebAssembly modules or an AI model being downloaded from eolietech.com. Those are downloads to you. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing goes to any other domain.
security.network.tip: Select a request and open its Payload tab to see what it sent. Code downloads send nothing.
security.offline.s1: Open a tool and process one file, so everything the tool needs has loaded.
security.offline.s2: Disconnect: turn on airplane mode, or choose Offline in the Network tab's throttling menu.
security.offline.s3: Process another file. It still works, because none of the work needs a server.
security.code.p1: Eolietech is open source under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0. The source repository holds the code of every tool and the headers file quoted above.

security.never.2: Show ads or load advertising scripts.
security.never.3: Sell or share data about you.
security.never.4: Ask for an account to use the free tools.

security.others.p2: The Pro waitlist on the pricing page uses Cloudflare Turnstile to keep out spam sign-ups. It loads on that page only.

guide.title: How to check if a website uploads your files | Eolietech
guide.description: A step-by-step way to tell whether an online converter or compressor uploads your files, using only your browser: the Network panel, an offline test and the Content-Security-Policy header.
guide.h1: Does this website upload your files?
guide.lede: Plenty of online converters promise to delete your files after an hour. Fewer can say they never receive them. With nothing but your browser, you can see which kind a site is.
guide.two.h2: Two ways a file tool can work
guide.two.p1: Most online file tools upload your file to their server, process it there and send the result back. Your file sits on someone else's computer for a while, and you have to trust what they say about deleting it.
guide.two.p2: Some tools do the work inside your browser instead, with code the page downloads to your device. The file is read from your disk into memory and the result is saved straight back. Nothing goes over the network, so there is nothing to delete.
guide.two.p3: On screen the two look the same: a drop zone, a progress bar, a download button. The checks below show the difference.
guide.network.p1: The Network panel in your browser's developer tools lists every request a page makes. If a site uploads your file, the upload has to show up there.
guide.network.s1: Open the tool's page on a computer, then open the developer tools: F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac.
guide.network.s2: Select the Network tab. Tick Preserve log, so the list survives a page reload, and clear what's already there.
guide.network.s3: Process a small test file, not one you care about.
guide.network.s4: Look for requests sent with the POST or PUT method (right-click the column headers to show the Method column). Select one and read its request headers: a Content-Length close to your file's size, or a content type such as multipart/form-data, means your file went with it.
guide.network.s5: Check where requests went, too. Uploads often go to a different address from the site itself, such as a cloud storage service.
guide.network.p2: Downloads are normal. The first time you use a tool, the page may fetch its code, WebAssembly modules or an AI model. Those come to you; what matters is what goes out.
guide.offline.s1: Open the tool and process one test file, so everything it needs has loaded.
guide.offline.s2: Go offline: turn on airplane mode, or choose Offline in the Network panel's throttling menu.
guide.offline.s3: Process another file. If it works, the work happens on your device. If the tool stops with a network error, it needed a server.
guide.offline.caveat: One catch: a page could hold on to the file and send it once you're back online. Keep the Network panel open when you reconnect and watch what goes out.
guide.csp.p1: A site can send a Content-Security-Policy header: rules your browser enforces on the page, whatever the page's own scripts try to do. Its connect-src rule lists the servers that scripts on the page may send data to.
guide.csp.p2: To see it, select the first request in the Network panel (the page itself) and find content-security-policy among the response headers. Or, from a terminal:
guide.csp.p3: connect-src 'self' means scripts can only talk to the site's own address. A list of other addresses means they can send data to those too. No policy, or a * in connect-src, means the browser sets no limit.
guide.csp.caveat: A strict connect-src is a strong sign, not proof. 'self' still allows the site's own server, so pair it with the Network panel test. And connect-src covers the usual ways scripts send data (fetch, XHR, WebSockets, beacons), not every possible one: loading an image or submitting a form can carry data as well, which is why a careful site also restricts img-src and form-action.
guide.limits.h2: What these checks can't tell you
guide.limits.1: What a server does with a file once it has one: how long it's kept, who can see it, what else it's used for. For that you only have the company's policy and your trust in it.
guide.limits.2: Whether the site changes tomorrow. A page can load different code on every visit, so a test covers the version you tested. Published source code and a strict policy make quiet changes harder.
guide.limits.3: What your browser extensions do. An extension allowed to read a page can see your files too, on any site.
guide.summary.network.value: No POST or PUT request carrying your file.
guide.summary.offline.value: The tool keeps working with the network off.
guide.summary.csp.value: connect-src limited to the site itself.
guide.summary.code.value: Published, so anyone can read what the page does.
guide.ours.p1: Eolietech's tools are built to pass every one of these checks. Its security page shows the exact policy the site sends and walks through the same tests on eolietech.com.
privacy.title: Privacy policy: what Eolietech keeps, and why | Eolietech
privacy.description: Your files never leave your device. The Eolietech privacy policy lists everything the site does handle: the Pro waitlist email, the spam check, hosting, and your rights under the GDPR.
privacy.lede: Your files never leave your device, so this list is short. Here is everything the site does handle, who handles it, and how to have it deleted.
privacy.short.files.value: Processed in your browser. Never uploaded, so we never have them.
privacy.short.waitlist.value: Only if you join: your email, the day you joined and which consent text you agreed to. Kept until Pro is announced, or until you ask us to delete it.
privacy.who.p1: The controller of the personal data described on this page is Francesco Basile, an individual based in Italy, who builds and runs Eolietech as candygoogy.
privacy.who.p2: Eolietech has not appointed a data protection officer, so your message goes straight to the person who runs the site. For anything about your data, write to:
privacy.files.h2: Your files stay on your device
privacy.files.p1: The tools open, convert and compress your files with code that runs in your browser. Your images, PDFs and audio are never sent to eolietech.com or to anyone else, so we can't see, keep or share them.
privacy.files.p2: Your browser enforces this. Every page is served with a Content-Security-Policy that includes connect-src 'self', which stops the page's scripts from connecting to any other server. The security page shows how to check it with your browser's developer tools.
privacy.browser.p1: The background remover and the audio transcriber run AI models. The first time you use one, your browser downloads the model files from eolietech.com and keeps them in its Cache Storage, so the next visit doesn't download them again. They are the same files for everyone and contain nothing about you.
privacy.browser.p2: Like with any website, your browser may also keep copies of the pages and the tools' code in its ordinary cache.
privacy.browser.p3: To remove all of it, delete the stored data for eolietech.com in your browser's settings. Most browsers list it under privacy, as site data or as cookies and site data. The only effect is that the models download again the next time you use those tools.
privacy.waitlist.h2: If you join the Pro waitlist
privacy.waitlist.p1: The waitlist on the pricing page is the only place the site asks for personal data. If you join, we store three things:
privacy.waitlist.kept.day: the day you joined (a date in UTC, with no time);
privacy.waitlist.kept.consent: which version of the waitlist text you agreed to, so we can show what you said yes to.
privacy.waitlist.p2: Nothing else goes in the list: no name, no IP address, no device details. Your IP address is used for a moment while you sign up, to limit repeated attempts from the same connection and to pass to the spam check described below. It is not saved in the waitlist.
privacy.waitlist.p3: We use your email address for one thing: to tell you when Pro launches. No newsletter, no other marketing, and we never sell or share the list.
privacy.waitlist.p4: The legal basis is your consent (Article 6(1)(a) GDPR). You can withdraw it at any time; that doesn't make our earlier use of your address unlawful.
privacy.waitlist.p5: We keep your entry until Pro has launched and the announcement has been sent, or until you ask to be removed, whichever comes first. Then we delete it.
privacy.waitlist.p6: The list is stored in a Cloudflare D1 database in Cloudflare's EU jurisdiction, so it stays inside the European Union. The sign-up code never writes your email address to a log; Cloudflare keeps technical logs of requests to the sign-up address for up to 7 days, so errors can be found.
privacy.waitlist.p7: There is no unsubscribe link yet. To leave the list, or to see or correct your entry, email us from the address you signed up with and we'll do it by hand:
privacy.turnstile.h2: The spam check on the pricing page
privacy.turnstile.p1: To keep bots off the waitlist, the form uses Cloudflare Turnstile. It loads only on the pricing page, and only once the form scrolls close to view. No other page loads it.
privacy.turnstile.p2: According to Cloudflare's Turnstile privacy addendum, Turnstile processes your IP address, a TLS fingerprint, your browser's user agent, and the site key and origin of the page, to tell people from bots. Cloudflare states that the purpose is not to identify, profile or target individuals.
privacy.turnstile.p3: Cloudflare handles these signals for us as a processor. It also acts as an independent controller when it uses them to improve Turnstile's bot detection.
privacy.turnstile.p4: The legal basis is our legitimate interest in keeping fake and abusive sign-ups off the list (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR).
privacy.hosting.p1: eolietech.com is hosted on Cloudflare, which acts as our processor. Like any web host, Cloudflare handles the data that comes with every request, such as your IP address, your browser's user agent and the address of the page, to deliver the site and protect it from attacks.
privacy.hosting.p2: The site runs no analytics scripts. The owner may look at the aggregated traffic statistics Cloudflare shows in its dashboard, such as how many requests the site received. They come from Cloudflare's normal handling of requests; nothing extra is collected for them.
privacy.hosting.p3: The legal basis is our legitimate interest in running a site that works and stays secure (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR).
privacy.email.p1: If you write to info@eolietech.com, we keep your message, your email address and whatever else you put in it, such as your name or an attachment. We use them only to read your message, answer it and do what you asked.
privacy.email.p2: Our mail is hosted by Fastmail Pty Ltd, a company based in Australia, which handles it for us as a processor under its data protection agreement.
privacy.email.p3: The legal basis is our legitimate interest in answering the people who write to us (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR). When you write to use one of your rights under the GDPR, answering is our legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c) GDPR).
privacy.email.p4: We keep the conversation for as long as it takes to deal with it, and delete it at the latest 12 months after the last message. You can ask us to delete it sooner.
privacy.never.1: Upload the files you open in a tool.
privacy.never.2: Set cookies, or keep anything in your browser besides the files described above.
privacy.never.3: Load analytics, tracking or advertising scripts.
privacy.never.4: Sell, rent or share your data for marketing.
privacy.never.5: Ask you to create an account.
privacy.transfers.p1: Cloudflare, Inc. is a US company with a worldwide network, so request data and Turnstile signals may be processed outside the European Union, including in the United States. Cloudflare states that it is certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, and that it relies on the standard contractual clauses if that certification lapses.
privacy.transfers.p2: The waitlist database itself is kept in Cloudflare's EU jurisdiction, as described above.
privacy.transfers.p3: Fastmail, our mail host, may transfer email data to other countries; its privacy policy names the United States, Australia and India among them. For data leaving the EU, Fastmail states that it uses the European Commission's standard contractual clauses.
privacy.rights.p1: Under the GDPR you have the right to:
privacy.rights.access: access the data we hold about you and get a copy of it;
privacy.rights.rectify: have it corrected if it's wrong;
privacy.rights.object: object to any use based on our legitimate interests;
privacy.rights.port: receive the data you gave us in a portable format;
privacy.rights.withdraw: withdraw your consent at any time, without affecting what happened before.
privacy.rights.p2: To use any of them, write to us. We answer within one month, and we may ask you to write from the address in question, so we know the request is really yours:
privacy.rights.p3: If you think we've handled your data wrongly, you can complain to the Italian data protection authority, the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, or to the authority of the EU country where you live.
privacy.rights.link: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
privacy.changes.p1: When this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it. If a change affects what you agreed to when you joined the waitlist, we'll ask for your consent again instead of assuming it.
terms.title: Terms of use | Eolietech
terms.description: The terms for using Eolietech's free browser tools: no account, nothing for sale, your files stay yours, the code is AGPL-3.0, and Italian law applies.
terms.lede: Free tools, no account, nothing for sale. These are the few rules that come with that, in type you can read.
terms.about.p1: These terms apply to eolietech.com and the tools on it. The site is run by Francesco Basile, an individual based in Italy, who goes by candygoogy online. By using the site you accept these terms; if you don't accept them, please don't use it.
terms.free.p1: The tools are free and need no account. There is nothing to buy on the site.
terms.free.p2: Pro doesn't exist yet. Joining the waitlist is not an order, a pre-order or a payment, and it commits neither of us to anything beyond the launch email described in the privacy policy. If Pro launches, it will come with its own terms, shown to you before you pay anything.
